steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an NLP paper studying which differential privacy budgets (epsilon) lay users would accept before donating sensitive text data. Motivate the gap, state the research question, and describe our survey study.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Sensitive data in NLP and differential privacy; gap: human perception ignored
2. Privacy budget epsilon and the open question of acceptable values
3. Risk perception differs among humans; research question
4. Our two-part survey study and hypothesis

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Context and gap
- sensitive data in NLP systems increasingly common
- differential privacy widely used for training NLP models or publishing data
- research mostly technical; human perception of privacy risks neglected

2. Privacy budget
- privacy risk of DP algorithm parametrized by \varepsilon>0, the privacy budget
- existing works consider appropriate \varepsilon values
- unknown: how lay users perceive risks, which \varepsilon acceptable in which situations
- "for which \varepsilon would you give us your textual data?"

3. Human risk perception; RQ
- DP makes no assumption on whether humans perceive privacy-loss risk the same way
- risk perception (esp. as probability) depends on various aspects, differs among humans
- RQ: optimal \varepsilon that lay users would accept and donate sensitive text data

4. Survey study
- two-part survey
- part 1: attitudes towards privacy + web-use skills (privacy concerns important factor in privacy-threatening decisions, prior work)
- part 2: behavioral experiment, repeated risk assessments in privacy-threatening situations
- two prototypical NLP scenarios: hypothetical collection of text medical records; chat history of an instant messenger
- goal: insights into RQ; hypothesis: decision-making modeled by a logistic function in this domain

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Using sensitive data in natural language processing (NLP) systems has become more and more common in recent years. Differential privacy is a method that is widely used to protect privacy when training NLP models or publishing data. But current research on differential privacy in NLP mostly looks at the technical side and neglects how humans perceive the privacy risks.

The privacy risk of a differentially private algorithm is parametrized by \varepsilon>0, which is the privacy budget. Existing works consider which \varepsilon values are appropriate, but we still don't know how lay users perceive privacy risks and which \varepsilon values they accept in which situations. In other words, for which \varepsilon would you give us your textual data?

Differential privacy does not make any assumptions about whether humans perceive the risk of privacy loss in the same way or not. But studies on how humans assess risks show that risk perception depends on various aspects and is different between humans, especially when the risk is given as a probability. So in this paper we ask the following research question. What is the optimal value of \varepsilon that lay users would accept and thus donate their sensitive text data?

We investigate this question systematically with a survey study that has two parts. In the first part, we measure the participants' attitudes towards privacy and also their web-use skills, as prior work shows that privacy concerns are an important factor when people make decisions in privacy-threatening situations. In the second part, we design, develop and conduct a behavioral experiment in which our participants repeatedly assess risks in privacy-threatening situations. We frame the risks in two prototypical NLP scenarios: a hypothetical collection of text medical records, and collecting the chat history of an instant messenger. The main goal of collecting data with the survey and the behavioral experiment is to get insights into our research question. We aim to confirm our hypothesis that human decision-making behavior in this domain can be modeled effectively by a logistic function.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The use of sensitive data in natural language processing (NLP) systems has become increasingly prevalent in recent years. Differential privacy is a widely-used method for privacy protection when training NLP models or publishing data [1,2,3,4,5]. However, current research on differential privacy in NLP focuses mainly on technical aspects, neglecting the human perception of privacy risks.

The privacy risk of a differentially private algorithm is parametrized by \varepsilon>0, the privacy budget. While existing works consider appropriate \varepsilon values [6,7,8,9,10], we still don't know how lay users perceive privacy risks and which \varepsilon values are acceptable in which situations. In other words, for which \varepsilon would you give us your textual data?

Differential privacy makes no assumptions about whether humans perceive the risk of privacy loss in the same way [11]. However, studies on human risk assessment show that the perception of risks, especially when conveyed as a probability, depends on various aspects and differs among humans [12]. In this paper we therefore ask the following research question: What is the optimal value of \varepsilon that lay users would accept and thus donate their sensitive text data?

We investigate this question systematically by conducting a two-part survey study. First, we measure participants' attitudes towards privacy as well as their web-use skills, as [7,10] show that privacy concerns are an important factor in decisions made in privacy-threatening situations. Second, we design, develop, and conduct a behavioral experiment involving repeated risk assessments by our participants in privacy-threatening situations. We frame the risks in two prototypical NLP scenarios, namely the hypothetical collection of text medical records and the collection of an instant messenger chat history. The primary objective of the survey and the behavioral experiment is to gain insights into our research question, with the aim of confirming our hypothesis that human decision-making behavior in this domain can be effectively modeled by a logistic function.
